social.title: Ballet Folclórico at the Palacio de Bellas Artes
social.description: Amalia Hernández's company has filled the Tiffany-curtained hall with whirling folk ballet for seventy years — the most joyful two hours in the building.
social.bonus: Arrive early to watch the Tiffany glass curtain reveal.

social.title: Mariachi Night at Plaza Garibaldi
social.description: The mariachi mothership — dozens of bands in full traje working the square every night. Commission a song, learn the grito, repeat.
social.bonus: Request a song for a stranger and dedicate it out loud.

social.title: Sunday Morning at Mercado El 100, Roma Norte
social.description: Every ingredient at this weekly organic market is certified grown within 100 kilometers of the city, and the producer conversations are as good as the produce.
social.bonus: Buy something from a vendor you've never cooked with before and ask them exactly how to prepare it.

social.title: Late Night Tacos at El Vilsito, Narvarte
social.description: By day it's an auto repair shop; by night the pit comes out and El Vilsito serves some of the city's best pastor to a line that doesn't form until well past midnight.
social.bonus: Order a full dorado — a flattened, crisped quesadilla — in addition to your tacos, and eat the entire thing standing on the street.

social.title: Long Lunch at Contramar, Colonia Roma
social.description: The legendary seafood restaurant on Durango has been packing in architects, artists, and politicians since 1998 — the tuna tostadas and grilled fish are non-negotiable.
social.bonus: Arrive without a reservation, wait at the bar, and use that time to befriend whoever is waiting next to you.

social.title: Rooftop Drinks at Hotel Downtown, Centro Histórico
social.description: A 16th-century colonial palace converted into a hotel has the best rooftop bar in Centro, with views straight down Cinco de Mayo toward the Zócalo as the city lights up.
social.bonus: Order a mezcal negroni and convince a stranger at the bar to point out one thing on the skyline you hadn't noticed.

social.title: Mezcal and Botanas at Cantina El Centenario, Coyoacán
social.description: This old-school cantina in Coyoacán serves complimentary botanas with every round in a tradition that most of the city has abandoned — Frida Kahlo drank in the neighborhood, not somewhere fancier.
social.bonus: Stay for three rounds without looking at your phone once — talk only to whoever is at the bar.

social.title: Night Walk on Calle Regina, Centro Histórico
social.description: This pedestrianized street in the heart of Centro comes alive after dark with mezcal bars, street food, cumbia blasting from open doorways, and zero tourists.
social.bonus: Accept a free tasting shot from any bar that offers one and then actually go inside and stay for at least one drink.

social.title: Happy Hour at Bar La Ópera, Centro Histórico
social.description: Order a brandy under the bullet hole Pancho Villa allegedly shot into the 19th-century ceiling of this gilded cantina that has outlasted every regime since 1876.
social.bonus: Ask the barman to point out the exact bullet hole, then convince your group on the spot whether it's real or a myth.

social.title: Lucha Libre at Arena México, Doctores
social.description: The cathedral of lucha libre hosts electrifying weekly bouts where masked legends and rising luchadores collide in front of a roaring crowd.
social.bonus: Learn one luchador's signature chant from a neighbor in the stands and lead the section in it at least once.

social.title: Jazz Night at Zinco Jazz Club, Centro Histórico
social.description: A 1930s bank vault converted into an underground jazz club — low ceilings, serious musicians, and mezcal cocktails in a room that feels like it was designed to make you stay until 3 a.m.
social.bonus: Strike up a conversation with the person next to you at the bar before the first set ends — make sure they're a stranger.

social.title: Pulque at La Hija de los Apaches, Guerrero
social.description: This century-old pulquería in Barrio de Guerrero pours thick, fermented agave sap straight from clay barrels into foam-flecked cups — the real Mexico City drink before mezcal was cool.
social.bonus: Ask the barman for a curado de apio — celery-cured pulque — and finish it before anyone at your table can try it.

social.title: Friday Night at Patrick Miller Disco, Centro
social.description: This legendary Friday-night hi-NRG dance hall in Centro has been running since the 1980s, and the regulars — dance-battling in circles for decades — will out-dance you without trying.
social.bonus: Get on the dance floor within the first 20 minutes and don't leave until a regular has taught you a move.

social.title: Sunday Night Mezcal Crawl Through Roma Norte
social.description: The blocks around Avenida Álvaro Obregón host some of the best mezcal bars in the world and Sunday night locals treat it as seriously as a Tuesday.
social.bonus: At your second bar, ask the mezcalero to pour you something they personally love that isn't on the menu.

foodie.title: Churros and Hot Chocolate at El Moro, Centro
foodie.description: Frying churros around the clock since 1935 — the tiled original on Eje Central at 2am is one of the city's great equalizers.
foodie.bonus: Go after midnight and order the Especial with extra chocolate for dunking.

foodie.title: Street Tlayuda at Mercado de Medellín, Colonia Roma
foodie.description: Buried in the back of Mercado de Medellín, a Oaxacan stall crisps massive corn tlayudas over a comal and loads them with tasajo, black beans, and quesillo right in front of you.
foodie.bonus: Wander the full market before eating — find three ingredients you've never seen and ask a vendor what they're for.

foodie.title: Tasting Counter at Sud 777, Pedregal
foodie.description: Edgar Núñez's jungle-garden restaurant in Pedregal makes hyperlocal Mexican tasting menus that feel grown rather than cooked — vegetables, herbs, and fungi sourced within 150 km.
foodie.bonus: Ask for the wine pairing, then tell the sommelier to swap any two pours for mezcal — see what they choose.

foodie.title: Torta at El Cuadrilátero, Centro Histórico
foodie.description: A lucha libre–themed sandwich counter that has been slinging absurdly overstuffed tortas since 1993 — the Gladiador with milanesa, chorizo, and avocado is a city landmark in edible form.
foodie.bonus: Order the largest torta on the menu and finish it solo in one sitting — no doggy bag.

foodie.title: Breakfast Chilaquiles at Lalo!, Roma Norte
foodie.description: Lalo! is the neighborhood breakfast institution that Roma Norte locals actually go to — loud, fast, perfectly executed chilaquiles with house salsa that hits every note.
foodie.bonus: Order the chilaquiles verdes extra spicy and eat them with zero sour cream, no modifications.

foodie.title: Dawn Breakfast at Fonda Margarita, Mixcoac
foodie.description: Open only until noon on weekdays, this legendary fonda in a family courtyard has served caldos, frijoles negros, and guisados from the same coal-fired stoves since 1964.
foodie.bonus: Show up before 8 a.m. and eat whatever the cook recommends without looking at the menu.

foodie.title: Tamales at Tamales Madre, Roma Norte
foodie.description: Tamales Madre reinvents the tamale as a serious gastronomic object — masa ground fresh daily, fillings that rotate by season, eaten at a marble counter that feels more like a wine bar than a street stall.
foodie.bonus: Pick the most unfamiliar filling on the menu and order two without asking what's in them.

foodie.title: Mole Negro at El Cardenal, Centro Histórico
foodie.description: Since 1969, El Cardenal has served the most meticulously sourced traditional Mexican breakfast and lunch in the city — their mole negro is a three-day recipe and tastes like it.
foodie.bonus: Order hot chocolate beaten tableside with a molinillo and drink every last drop before your food arrives.

foodie.title: Carnitas at El Bajío, Azcapotzalco
foodie.description: Carmen Titita's legendary 50-year-old Mexican kitchen serves carnitas so rich and crispy they've earned a cult following that crosses every class line in the city.
foodie.bonus: Order the maciza and buche on a single taco and eat it standing at the counter without a napkin.

foodie.title: Tasting Menu at Pujol
foodie.description: Enrique Olvera's mole madre — some batches aged over 1,000 days — is one of the most discussed dishes in the world and you eat it here in Polanco.
foodie.bonus: Ask the server exactly how many days old tonight's mole madre is and remember the number.

foodie.title: Breakfast at Café de Tacuba
foodie.description: Open since 1912, this baroque dining room in Centro Histórico serves chilaquiles and chocolate caliente under hand-painted tiles that haven't changed in a century.
foodie.bonus: Order everything in Spanish, including asking the waiter what he recommends, and don't switch to English once.

foodie.title: Eat Tacos de Canasta at El Farolito, Condesa
foodie.description: El Farolito has been feeding Mexico City at 3am since 1952 and the tacos here — crispy, grease-edged, relentless — are what the city actually tastes like.
foodie.bonus: Order the campechano and eat it standing at the counter without using a single napkin.

chill.title: Tour Casa Luis Barragán
chill.description: The UNESCO-listed house of Mexico's greatest architect is a masterclass in light, color, and silence — small guided groups only, and worth every peso of the booking hassle.
chill.bonus: Reserve weeks ahead; photograph nothing and remember everything.

chill.title: Morning at Casa Azul — the Frida Kahlo Museum
chill.description: Frida's cobalt-blue Coyoacán house holds her studio, her dresses, and her garden exactly as she left them — book the first slot and beat the world to it.
chill.bonus: Buy tickets online days ahead — walk-ups get turned away.

chill.title: Sit With the Murals at Palacio de Bellas Artes
chill.description: The interior of Mexico City's most beautiful building holds Rivera, Orozco, Siqueiros, and Tamayo murals within a single art deco marble hall — and almost nobody sits long enough to really look.
chill.bonus: Pick one mural, sit directly in front of it for fifteen uninterrupted minutes, and write three sentences about what you see.

chill.title: Morning Market Crawl at Mercado Jamaica
chill.description: The country's largest wholesale flower market floods with color before 7 a.m. and the chaos of vendors, buckets, and fragrance is unlike anywhere else in the city.
chill.bonus: Buy a single stem from three different vendors, combine them into a bouquet, and give it away to a stranger outside.

chill.title: Afternoon at Museo Nacional de Antropología
chill.description: The greatest pre-Columbian collection on earth sits in Chapultepec and rewards slow, unguided wandering — the Aztec Sun Stone alone is worth the trip.
chill.bonus: Find the Olmec colossal head in the Gulf Coast Hall and sketch its face in your phone notes using only emoji.

chill.title: Sunset at Mirador del Cerro del Tepeyac, Gustavo A. Madero
chill.description: Above the Basílica de Guadalupe, the hilltop path to the original chapel rewards the climb with a sweeping north-city panorama almost no tourist bothers to reach.
chill.bonus: Walk the full hill circuit, stop at every chapel en route, and light a candle at the oldest one you can find.

chill.title: Murals at the Secretaría de Educación Pública, Centro
chill.description: The SEP building holds 235 Diego Rivera murals painted between 1923 and 1928 — free to enter, almost never crowded, and arguably the most important mural cycle in Mexican history.
chill.bonus: Find the panel where Rivera painted himself into the scene and take a photo from the same angle he used as reference.

chill.title: Slow Morning at Parque México, Condesa
chill.description: The oval Art Deco park at the heart of Colonia Condesa is a masterclass in civilized city life — fountains, fountains, art deco lamp posts, and the best people-watching in any colonia.
chill.bonus: Buy a coffee from a passing vendor and claim a bench near the amphitheater — stay until you've heard at least three different languages.

chill.title: Rooftop Sunset at Torre Latinoamericana, Centro
chill.description: The 44th-floor observation deck of this 1956 Art Deco skyscraper delivers a 360-degree panorama of the entire Valley of Mexico — smog permitting, you see five volcanoes at once.
chill.bonus: Time your visit to arrive exactly at sunset and stay up top until you can count five visible light clusters of distinct neighborhoods in the darkness.

chill.title: Stroll Through the Viveros de Coyoacán
chill.description: This government tree nursery turned public park is where Coyoacán joggers, dog walkers, and elderly chess players live their best slow morning — massive ahuehuete trees shade paths that feel miles from the city.
chill.bonus: Find a bench deep in the nursery grid, sit for 20 minutes without your phone, and count how many bird species you hear.

chill.title: Coffee at Café Avellaneda, Coyoacán
chill.description: This tiny specialty roaster tucked inside a Coyoacán courtyard pulls some of the most precise espresso in the city from single-origin Mexican beans — locals queue for it every morning.
chill.bonus: Order a black espresso and drink it in two sips at the bar, Italian-style, no chair.

chill.title: Afternoon at Museo Dolores Olmedo, Xochimilco
chill.description: A colonial hacienda in Xochimilco housing the world's largest private collection of Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo works — roamed by real peacocks and a colony of hairless Xoloitzcuintli dogs.
chill.bonus: Find the Xolo dog and sit on the grass near it until it comes to you — no treats, no coaxing.

chill.title: Read at Librería El Péndulo, Polanco
chill.description: This multi-story bookshop-café has been a Polanco institution since 1991 — the garden terrace, the coffee, and the complete lack of urgency are the whole point.
chill.bonus: Buy a book in Spanish entirely based on its cover and read the first page before you order your coffee.

chill.title: Afternoon in the Jardín Centenario, Coyoacán
chill.description: Coyoacán's central plaza has been the neighborhood's living room for four centuries — sit under the laurel trees, buy an esquite, and let the afternoon collapse.
chill.bonus: Pick one stranger to observe for ten minutes and invent their entire life story in your head before you leave.

active.title: Hike the River Canyon at Los Dinamos
active.description: A protected canyon inside the city limits where the Magdalena — the capital's last living river — runs cold and clear under pine forest, with trout quesadillas at the trailhead.
active.bonus: Order the river trout at a trailside comedor afterward.

active.title: Dance Danzón at Plaza de la Ciudadela
active.description: Every Saturday afternoon the plaza fills with couples dancing danzón the way they have for fifty years — the regulars will teach you the steps if you stand still long enough.
active.bonus: Accept the first dance invitation you get.

active.title: Sunrise Tai Chi at Parque Hundido, Insurgentes
active.description: Every morning a dedicated group of regulars runs an open tai chi session inside this sunken Art Deco park, and strangers are always quietly welcomed in.
active.bonus: Mirror the instructor's full sequence from start to finish without breaking form or checking your phone.

active.title: Lap Swim at Alberca Olímpica Francisco Márquez, Chapultepec
active.description: This 1968 Olympics-era outdoor pool sits inside Chapultepec and offers open public lanes where serious swimmers have been training under open sky for decades.
active.bonus: Swim one full kilometer without stopping — that's 20 lengths of a 50m pool.

active.title: Morning Run Along Canal Nacional, Iztapalapa
active.description: The old pre-Hispanic canal that once connected Tenochtitlán to the lake system still runs for kilometers through the south of the city, and the early morning path belongs entirely to locals.
active.bonus: Run the full 5km stretch from start to end without stopping, then reward yourself with an atole from the nearest street cart.

active.title: Mountain Bike the Desierto de los Leones Trails
active.description: The pine forests of this high-altitude national park just outside the city offer 17th-century ruins, real elevation, and singletrack that rewards anyone willing to rent a bike and climb.
active.bonus: Reach the ruined Carmelite convent on two wheels without putting a foot down on the final climb.

active.title: Dawn Row at Lago de Chapultepec
active.description: Rent a rowboat at first light when the lake is mirror-still and the park belongs entirely to you and a few old men fishing from the banks.
active.bonus: Row to the dead center of the lake, ship your oars, and sit in total silence for two full minutes.

active.title: Outdoor Yoga at Parque Lincoln, Polanco
active.description: Polanco's leafy Art Deco park hosts free outdoor yoga sessions under the jacaranda trees on weekend mornings — join locals who treat this as a non-negotiable weekly ritual.
active.bonus: Introduce yourself to the instructor after class and ask them to name one pose you did wrong — actually fix it.

active.title: Trail Run in Bosque de Tlalpan
active.description: A vast semi-wild forest in the south of the city offers 20 km of unpaved trails through pine and oak — Mexico City's best urban escape for anyone who needs dirt under their shoes.
active.bonus: Run without a GPS route — enter at the main gate and find your way back using only landmarks and trail signs.

active.title: Cycle the Paseo de la Reforma on Sunday Morning
active.description: Every Sunday the city closes its grandest boulevard to cars and cyclists take it over end-to-end — it's the fastest and most cinematic way to feel the scale of CDMX.
active.bonus: Ride the full length from Chapultepec to the Zócalo without stopping and time yourself.

adventure.title: Climb the Monumento a la Revolución
adventure.description: Take the glass elevator up the world's tallest triumphal arch, then walk the open-air dome galleries where the whole Centro spreads out beneath you.
adventure.bonus: Find your hotel or Airbnb from the observation deck.

adventure.title: Ride the Cablebús Over the Rooftops of Cuautepec
adventure.description: Mexico City's cable car glides for miles over painted rooftops and mountainside barrios — the best civic-infrastructure joyride in the Americas costs less than a coffee.
adventure.bonus: Ride to the last station and back without checking your phone once.

adventure.title: Ride a Trajinera Through the Canals of Xochimilco
adventure.description: Board a painted party barge at Embarcadero Nuevo Nativitas and drift the last living canals of the Aztec chinampas while floating mariachis pull up alongside.
adventure.bonus: Buy a song from a passing mariachi boat — full volume, no shame.

adventure.title: Take a Boat to Isla de las Muñecas, Xochimilco
adventure.description: The Island of the Dolls is a genuine fever dream — thousands of decaying dolls hung in trees by a caretaker who believed they held a drowned girl's spirit.
adventure.bonus: Hang a doll you've brought from home on the island and say something aloud to it before you leave.

adventure.title: Walk the Rooftop Trail at Museo Anahuacalli
adventure.description: Diego Rivera's lava-stone pyramid museum in Coyoacán has a rooftop terrace with panoramic views and almost nobody ever goes up there.
adventure.bonus: Find the small window on the top level that frames Popocatépetl on a clear day and take a photo through it.

adventure.title: Explore Mercado de La Lagunilla on Sunday
adventure.description: This sprawling Sunday flea market in Centro spills across streets with antiques, street food, vintage lucha masks, and zero tourist curation.
adventure.bonus: Negotiate the price of something down by at least 40% and actually buy it.

adventure.title: Wander the Labyrinths of Bosque de Chapultepec
adventure.description: The largest urban park in the Americas hides forests, ruins, a zoo, and lakes that most visitors never find past the first gate.
adventure.bonus: Navigate to Section 3 without using your phone and find the Moctezuma Aqueduct ruins before noon.

adventure.title: Walk the Digs at Templo Mayor
adventure.description: Beneath the ruins of the Aztec empire's holiest site, archaeologists are still pulling gods out of the earth and you can walk right up to the dig.
adventure.bonus: Find the offering cache labeled Cala 4 and sketch one object from it in your notes app before leaving.

adventure.title: Kayak the Canals of Xochimilco
adventure.description: The ancient chinampas float past as you paddle through the last living remnant of the Aztec lake system on a trajinera you actually steer yourself.
adventure.bonus: Pull over at a chinampa farm, step off the boat, and ask the farmer if you can pick something from the soil.

adventure.title: Walk the Avenue of the Dead at Teotihuacán
adventure.description: One of the largest pyramids on earth rises over the Avenue of the Dead — the climb is closed these days, but standing beneath the Sun Pyramid at opening hour is still the most ancient thing you can do before lunch.
adventure.bonus: Reach the very top before 9am and sit in silence for five full minutes before anyone else arrives.
